sections.html:
Hillsboro's Administration Center, 729 Maple Street, houses all three offices you may need. One values each parcel (Assessor), one runs the first-level appeal board (County Clerk), and one sends out the bills and takes payment (Collector).

  • Assessor: 636-797-5343 for real estate, 636-797-5466 for personal property, office hours are 8 am to 5 pm, Monday to Friday.
  • County Clerk: 636-797-5478 for Board of Equalization appointments.
  • Collector: 636-797-5406, mailing address P.O. Box 100, Hillsboro, MO 63050.

None of these offices sets your rate. School, fire, ambulance and other districts do that for the land inside their boundaries, so two houses in different school districts, say Fox C-6 and Hillsboro R-3, can have quite different totals.

Jefferson County is a Mississippi River county just south of St. Louis. Arnold has the most people, Hillsboro is where the courthouse sits, and the incorporated places also include Festus, De Soto, Crystal City, Herculaneum and Pevely. As of July 2025 there were 233,132 residents and 96,228 housing units. More than four in five homes are owner-occupied (82.2%), with a median value of $237,200.

Since so many households own, many tax bills are paid by mortgage servicers out of escrow. If that is you, the lender-request rule under due dates, below, matters.

sections.h2: How the Assessor values a home
sections.html:
The Assessor relies on mass appraisal. Building replacement cost less depreciation, plus land value, gives fair market value. Every parcel in Missouri is reassessed in odd-numbered years, which makes 2027 the coming cycle. The county then applies a percentage that depends on the property class.

Assessment levels used in Jefferson County
Property classShare of market value taxed
Residential19%
Commercial32%
Agricultural12%

A bill can move even without a reassessment. Adding a garage or an adjoining acre lifts assessed value, as does completing a house that was prorated during construction. A levy change approved by voters alters the total even if your value is unchanged.

The tax is due by December 31 and delinquent from January 1. November brings the bills, first on the county website and then in the mail. Call the Collector if December 1 comes and goes with no bill, because the deadline still applies to you.

  • Pay at 729 Maple Street, online, or or by calling 1-877-289-0099. Cards, debit or credit, add a 2.5% convenience fee with a $1.95 minimum; an e-check adds $4.95.
  • For mail, the postmark must read December 31 or earlier. Ask your post office when its final pickup is.
  • A mortgage company has to send the Collector a written request for each bill it intends to pay. If a paper bill reached you, your lender never made that request.

The Collector cannot waive penalty or interest, a limit tied to section 139.100 and an Attorney General opinion. RSMo 140.100 adds an 18 percent penalty for each delinquent year on land in the back tax book, and land redeemed before the sale can be charged no more than 2 percent per month.

Your first step is to phone the Assessor, whose appraiser will talk through the value and weigh anything you can show. A disagreement that survives that conversation goes to the Board of Equalization, and you file through the County Clerk. Each year the cutoff is the second Monday in July; in 2027 that is July 12.

  1. Ask the Assessor, 636-797-5343, for an informal review.
  2. Get forms and a hearing date from the County Clerk, 636-797-5478.
  3. Bring five copies of any written evidence: one per board member, one for the board secretary and one for the Assessor.
  4. A certified letter with the decision typically follows within 5 business days.
  5. Still unhappy? File a Complaint for Review of Assessment with the State Tax Commission and include the board's decision letter.

Commission filings are due September 30, or 30 days from the board's decision if that comes later, counted from the letter's date. An LLC, trust, corporation or estate must use an attorney to file.

The bill is still due December 31 while an appeal is pending. Paying under protest means full payment ahead of the delinquency date plus a written statement giving your grounds and your own figure for fair market value. The word protest scribbled on a check does nothing alone.

Homeowners can look at two programs. Jefferson County has a Real Property Tax Credit for Seniors, enacted February 15, 2024, and the Assessor can explain it. The state also offers a Property Tax Credit Claim that gives back part of the real estate tax or rent paid over the year.

  • State credit maximums are $1,100 for owner-occupants and $750 for renters.
  • Eligibility: age 65 by December 31 of the prior year, 100% disability for you or your spouse, or age 60 or older with surviving spouse benefits.
  • Income limits, counting Social Security, are $30,000 for a single person and $34,000 for married homeowners.
  • File form MO-1040 with schedule MO-PTS, or form MO-PTC if you do not file an income tax return.

If a tornado, flood, fire or earthquake destroys your house, you can ask the Assessor to remove the residential value pro rata under section 137.082. Use the Destroyed Residential Property form.

At most closings the seller's share of the year's tax is credited on the settlement statement, and the buyer takes on the whole year's bill. Your settlement statement or title company shows the actual split.

A new deed recorded at the Recorder of Deeds office is what changes the owner in the Assessor's file. Names on real estate bills change only through a recorded deed, so a phone call alone will not update the owner or the mailing address.

  1. Ask the Collector for the amount due on every year, penalty and interest included, before you accept an offer.
  2. Give that figure to the title company so it can pay the balance from your proceeds.
  3. Confirm that your lender's escrow, if you have one, covers the current bill so it is not paid twice.

If your closing lands near the end of the year, ask the title company which bill it expects to pay and by what date, since the December 31 cutoff can fall between contract and closing. A cash sale follows the same path. The buyer's funds go through title, the delinquent years are paid first, and you keep what is left. Repairs and a lender's appraisal do not hold up the tax payoff.

faqs.q: By what date must a Jefferson County real estate bill be paid?
faqs.a: December 31 of the tax year. A payment postmarked later is charged penalty and interest, and the Collector cannot waive either one.

faqs.q: When is the Jefferson County appeal deadline?
faqs.a: The Board of Equalization takes filings until the second Monday in July. Missouri reassesses in odd-numbered years, so the next notices arrive in 2027 with a July 12, 2027 filing date.

faqs.q: Who do I call if my Jefferson County tax bill never arrived?
faqs.a: Call the Collector at 636-797-5406. Owners should call if nothing shows up by December 1, and the December 31 deadline stays the same either way.

faqs.q: Does my mortgage lender pay the Jefferson County bill?
faqs.a: Only if it sent the Collector a written request for your bill. If the paper bill came to you, the lender did not ask for it, so ask the lender where it wants the bill sent.

faqs.q: Who pays the year's tax when I sell my Jefferson County house?
faqs.a: Usually the seller's portion is credited at closing and the buyer owes the whole year's bill. Your settlement statement lays out the split.
